newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish government vote raises market optimism.
newsitem.headline: Turkish government vote raises market optimism.

text.p: Istanbul shares rose on Wednesday on expectations the Islamist-led government would be able to function once more after weeks of uncertainty over an opposition challenge, brokers said.

"If the government is going to stay, if it wants to stay, this is a sign that they are going to do something, that is, that something is going to change. This decreases the uncertainty and tension and this reflects positively on the market," Cagdas Menkul General Manager Berki Ozmen told Reuters.
Istanbul shares firmed in early trade on Wednesday, with the IMKB National-100 ending the morning session 12 points, or 0.79 percent higher than Tuesday's close at 1,522.
"It will be difficult for the index to fall...In the short term I think it will go up," Ozmen said.
Late on Tuesday, Parliament voted 271-265 in favour of dropping a censure motion against the government of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, Turkey's first Islamist leader.

But Bumerang General Manager Alp Tekince warned that turbulent times may not be over yet. Immediately following the opposition's failure to dislodge Erbakan, a top prosecutor called on the constitutional court to outlaw his Welfare Party.
"The developments relating to the demand to close Welfare could create uncertainty in the market in the medium term," Tekince said.
Legal experts have said that it would take at least six months for the Welfare case to produce a result.

The stock market has fallen consistently over the past month as the secularist opposition, media and the powerful army increased pressure on Erbakan's alliance with the conservatives, culminating in the filing of the censure motion last week.
The market had been expecting the government to go because it had been hounded to the point where it could not function.

Brokers say they hope the government will now be able to work on fulfilling some of its economic promises, such as pushing ahead with delayed privatisations, reforming the social security system and making other medium-term structural changes.

They were also heartened by rumours that deputy prime minister Tansu Ciller, a pro-Western free-market advocate, would become prime minister soon under a rotating premiership agreement with Erbakan. She had been due to take up the post next year.

"Now there are new expectations -- one is to do with the government's make-up, the other to do with the government's actions. The market is buying this," Deha Menkul Degerler general manager of Bihlun Tamayligil told Reuters.
"The process of change in the government and after that, expectations surrounding privatisation, are sparking buying," Tamayligil said.
Mustafa Yilmaz, chairman of Mustafa Yilmaz Securities, said market players had to begin taking more note of economic news and be less at the mercy of political events.

"Political problems worry the stock market. A false agenda had been created in which the market was expected to rise when the government fell, but in fact it stabilised when the government didn't go," he told Reuters.
"Industrialists, businessmen are continuing with their investments. It is time to understand that company profits have nothing to do with the government," he said.
